claims.text: The high corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by rapid formation and continuous regeneration of a chromium oxide passivation layer.
The protective passivation layer is Cr2O3.
A chromium content of at least 10 wt% is representative of steels designed for harsh chemical-processing or nuclear environments.
Mo and Ni additions are used alongside Cr in the proposed high-performance stainless or duplex steels.
Controlled pre-oxidation initiates or promotes passivation.
Controlled pH and oxygen concentrations can favor formation of Cr2O3 under the proposed test conditions.
The thickness, continuity, and adhesion of the Cr2O3 layer govern its performance as an electronic and ionic barrier.
Chromium in the alloy oxidizes rapidly at the steel surface in corrosive environments.
Surface oxidation of chromium forms a thin, adherent Cr2O3 film.
The Cr2O3 film limits transport of oxygen and aggressive ions into the underlying metal.
Limiting oxygen and aggressive-ion transport reduces the overall corrosion rate.
The Cr2O3 passivation layer can self-heal after minor damage, improving long-term protection.
Steels forming a continuous and robust Cr2O3 film will have lower corrosion current density, higher EIS impedance, and less weight loss than low-Cr or passivation-disrupted steels.
Steels with lower chromium content or inhibited passivation will have higher corrosion rates under otherwise identical conditions.
Sufficient alloy chromium is required to form the proposed passivating oxide.
The proposed mechanism may not operate in highly reducing environments because oxide formation is not thermodynamically favored there.
Mo and Ni content can influence the relationship between chromium content, oxide properties, and corrosion rate.
Temperature, pH, and oxygen level can influence the relationship between chromium content, oxide properties, and corrosion rate.

contradictions.description: The intervention describes the non-pre-oxidized comparison samples as retaining their native surface condition, whereas the falsification design says that the comparison group has its native surface oxide removed. These are materially different controls.
